newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia lacks political will to reform, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Serbia lacks political will to reform, analysts say.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic is expected to reshuffle and reduce his government next week but analysts believe he is not yet prepared to embark on the road to genuine reform.
"This is just a cosmetic change," one Western diplomat said on Thursday. "I doubt that he will get rid of his hardliners and bite the bullet by launching radical reforms, including privatisation."
"There is still no political readiness for any major changes of the existing system," the diplomat told Reuters.
Local media earlier announced there would be a government reshuffle cutting the cabinet from 31 to 23 members, but names being mentioned did not suggest any significant change of policy was likely.

Milosevic, under pressure from 12 weeks of opposition protests demanding he recognise their gains in local elections last November, had personally demanded cuts in the government to improve its efficiency, political sources said.
But merely reducing its size without appointing forceful pro-reform champions is unlikely to produce any positive results, anlaysts said.

Most of the current cabinet members are also managers of major state-owned firms, most of them running at a loss, and are unwilling to initiate reform which could force them to lay off workers or close them down.
"Milosevic is trying to score points at home after his popularity plunged, especially after police intervened against peaceful protesters last week-end," one Wester diplomat said.
"This might improve his image at home but not abroad," the diplomat said. "The West is not deceived by his move."
Milosevic, in desperate need for fresh foreign funds to revitalise the ailing economy, is also under increasing pressure from various social groups and workers to pay wages.
Local analysts say foreign investors will be very reluctant to come here without a firm political decision on political and economic reforms.

"The monopoly of political and economic powers must be broken if Milosevic wants fresh funds from abroad," Danica Popovic, analyst of the private CES-Mecon institute for econimic studies, told Reuters.
Analysts agree that the current process of privatisation is largely a sham aimed at attracting foreign and local investors.
"Privatisation is the stumbling block," another Western envoy said. "Changing the size of the government will not improve the country's international image or attract foreign investors."
